title: The 2026 Qualifying and race head-to-heads so far
excerpt:
As the 2026 season continues, F1.com assesses how the team mate head-to-heads have stacked up so far. Who from each of the 11 pairings on the grid has had the upper hand in Qualifying and/or race trim across the campaign? Let’s take a look at the numbers…

Mercedes

Qualifying: Russell 7-11 Antonelli

Race: Russell 5-13 Antonelli

Perhaps unsurprisingly given his hold on the top spot in the Drivers’ Championship, Kimi Antonelli has also taken the lead when it comes to the head-to-head statistics at Mercedes. The Italian has beaten George Russell in Qualifying 11 times out of 18, with seven of those occasions seeing him take pole position.

The numbers are similar in the race day figures, Antonelli having crossed the line ahead of Russell at 13 Grands Prix – and winning at nine of them. Russell on the other hand has experienced marginally more bad luck, recording three DNFs in comparison to one for Antonelli.

Antonelli’s latest victory in Austin last time out, combined with Russell’s P8 finish, means the sophomore racer now leads the championship by a whopping 123 points.

Ferrari

Qualifying: Leclerc 10-8 Hamilton

Race: Leclerc 9-9 Hamilton

Over at Ferrari, there is little to choose between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton on both counts.

Hamilton pulled back level with Leclerc on Qualifying stats after his front row start in Malaysia, before Leclerc edged ahead again in Singapore and Austin. On race days, the pair are now equal following Leclerc's podium result at the United States Grand Prix.

McLaren

Qualifying: Norris 11-7 Piastri

Race: Norris 10-7 Piastri*

*No mark included for the Chinese Grand Prix as both drivers failed to start

In the Qualifying statistics between Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, Norris leads with 11 better results. This includes his pole positions at the Hungarian, Dutch and Spanish Grands Prix.

The McLaren pair aren't too far apart in race day figures, although Norris has recorded three DNFs, while Piastri has one to his name as well as a DNS from the season opener in Australia (not including the Chinese Grand Prix where both recorded a DNS). Norris is responsible for the squad's two victories so far at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort.

Red Bull

Qualifying: Verstappen 11-4 Hadjar

Qualifying: Verstappen 3-0 Lawson

Race: Verstappen 12-3 Hadjar

Race: Verstappen 2-1 Lawson

Isack Hadjar faced the difficult task of stepping up as Max Verstappen’s new team mate at Red Bull in 2026 – and while he has enjoyed a solid campaign until now, it is the Dutchman that leads the way in the statistics.

Verstappen has out-qualified his team mate on 14 occasions (including Liam Lawson’s super-sub stint), as well as finishing ahead on race day 14 times. The four-time World Champion recorded retirements at the other three events, one more DNF than the two experienced by Hadjar.

The Frenchman was unexpectedly replaced by Racing Bulls’ Lawson for three Grands Prix after sustaining a wrist injury.

Verstappen claimed his and Red Bull’s first pole position and victory of the season in Malaysia, before going back-to-back in Singapore – an event he had never previously won.

Racing Bulls

Qualifying: Lawson 9-6 Lindblad

Qualifying: Tsunoda 0-3 Lindblad

Race: Lawson 11-4 Lindblad

Race: Tsunoda 1-2 Lindblad

Racing Bulls have enjoyed a strong season in 2026, with both drivers performing well. However, it is Lawson who has taken the lead in the head-to-heads, albeit narrowly in Qualifying form – the New Zealander holding the edge by nine to six over Arvid Lindblad.

Lawson has finished ahead of Lindblad at 11 out of the 15 Grands Prix they have contested together as team mates, though the gap between the duo – who have recorded six double points finishes so far – has often been small. There has been one retirement so far for Lawson (in Miami), while Lindblad did not start in Canada due to a clutch issue.

Alpine

Qualifying: Gasly 15-3 Colapinto

Race: Gasly 11-6 Colapinto *No mark for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as both drivers retired

Pierre Gasly has been dominant in the Qualifying statistics at Alpine, having beaten Franco Colapinto by 15 to three.

He even grabbed his maiden pole position at Monza, completely on merit in a dry session as the upgraded Alpine took the fight to the top teams.

The picture is a little more even on race day, where Gasly’s lead is now 11 over Colapinto’s six.

Haas

Qualifying: Bearman 13-5 Ocon

Race: Bearman 10-7 Ocon*

*No mark for the Dutch Grand Prix as both drivers retired

At Haas, Ollie Bearman has qualified ahead of Esteban Ocon on 13 occasions. The Briton’s best Saturday result so far was a P10 in China and Azerbaijan.

Bearman has the advantage in Grand Prix finishes too, beating Ocon by 10 to seven. In terms of reliability, Bearman has suffered five DNFs, with Ocon experiencing his first of the year in Zandvoort where neither were able to finish the race.

Ocon achieved his best result of the season with a P8 in Azerbaijan, and Bearman’s P9 meant Haas secured their first double points finsh of the campaign.

Audi

Qualifying: Hulkenberg 9-9 Bortoleto

Race: Hulkenberg 10-8 Bortoleto

Audi drivers Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto are evenly matched when it comes to Qualifying performances, with Bortoleto claiming the team's best starting position of P8 at the Belgian Grand Prix.

The younger driver has enjoyed slightly better luck in terms of reliability; Bortoleto has crossed the line at every race barring China (where he failed to start) and Singapore, while Hulkenberg has suffered three DNFs along with a DNS in Australia.

Williams

Qualifying: Albon 5-13 Sainz

Race: Albon 7-11 Sainz

It has been a tough campaign so far for Williams, who remain down in P9 of the Teams’ Championship. While there has not been much to celebrate, Carlos Sainz might take heart from the fact that he leads the Qualifying head-to-head by 13 to five over Alex Albon.

That does not quite tell the full story, though, with Albon offering his team mate a tow in Monza to ensure Sainz made it to Q2, while the latter lost a top-10 start in Baku due to a grid penalty.

Sainz also tops the Grand Prix figures, by 11 to seven. Points have been a rarity for the team, with the Spaniard recording three P9 finishes, and most recently a P10 in Baku with a heavily-upgraded car, while Albon has a P8 and a P10 to his name.

Aston Martin

Qualifying: Alonso 16-2 Stroll

Race: Alonso 10-3 Stroll*

*No mark for the Australian, Chinese, Barcelona, Italian and Azerbaijan Grands Prix as both drivers retired

Like Williams, Aston Martin have endured a challenging 2026. Such were the squad’s car issues that neither driver was able to finish the opening two rounds in Australia and China, while both also retired with reliability problems in Barcelona and Baku. However, substantial upgrades to the car and power unit have offered encouraging signs of progress.

In terms of the head-to-heads, Fernando Alonso has outscored Lance Stroll on both counts – albeit by a lesser extent on Sundays – and the Spaniard is also responsible for the team’s points, as he finished P10 in Monaco, P9 in the Netherlands, and P8 in Malaysia.

Cadillac

Qualifying: Perez 10-8 Bottas

Race: Perez 12-4 Bottas*

*No mark for the Austrian and Hungarian Grands Prix as both drivers retired

Cadillac recruited the experienced pairing of Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez for the squad’s maiden F1 season – and while the duo have often been fighting towards the rear of the pack, they are closely matched on Qualifying head-to-heads.

The Mexican holds the advantage in the Grand Prix statistics, finishing ahead of Bottas on 12 occasions. Both drivers have suffered their fair share of reliability concerns, with the Finn retiring from nine races, while Perez is on five DNFs.

title: How ‘everything went wrong’ for Red Bull in United States GP
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar shared a collective disappointment in their inability to fight for more points at the United States Grand Prix, with the Dutchman concluding that Red Bull faced “too many issues”.

Following his back-to-back victories in Malaysia and Singapore, Verstappen qualified in second place at the Circuit of The Americas as Hadjar took third, matching his best-ever Qualifying result.

Verstappen angled his RB22 for an aggressive start to pass polesitter Kimi Antonelli, but his launch instead left him at the mercy of Ferrari and he dropped behind Charles Leclerc before fighting his way back past.

From there, he pitted twice and took advantage of Lando Norris’ struggles on ageing tyres to reclaim P2 once again, although Leclerc ultimately demoted him to third in the closing stages of the race.

“We didn’t have the pace of Kimi,” Verstappen said. “At the same time I think the way we used our tyres, the order, was wrong – probably also the wrong compounds in hindsight, but that’s something to still understand because lately, the harder compounds have not been competitive and now suddenly they were.

“From our side, I think there were too many issues with the power unit unfortunately in terms of consistency. You can’t rely on a consistent balance through a corner because if every lap and every corner it’s doing something different, it’s very hard to be on top of things.

“A slow pit stop was also very costly today, so a few things to analyse and do better.

“It’s going to be a bit hit or miss, I guess – two really good weekends where we were on top of things, and here we weren’t on top of things. Different layout, of course, where you have a bit more high-speed corners. It seemed like we were not fantastic in the high-speed corners.”

Hadjar wasn’t best pleased either, having dropped to P5 on the opening lap with similar difficulties linked to his launch. He managed to improve back to the top three with an extended soft-tyre stint, but was ordered to let his team mate overtake him once Verstappen had moved onto fresh rubber.

When Hadjar eventually peeled into the pits, he got stuck on the incorrect engine mapping and faced a throttle problem as a result, which impacted his performance on the way to finishing P6.

He explained: “Everything went wrong. First of all, the race start – I did everything on my side. I had a clutch overdelivery so it was completely out of my control again. It’s really starting to p*** me off.

“It’s not a nice feeling when you know you're going to drop the clutch, you don’t know what you’re going to have. Today was very poor. That first stint was very strong. I kept extending. I had the pace of Kimi towards those last couple of laps, so I was quite confident. I was blocked on a pit stop throttle map, it was just undriveable and that was it for me.

“I’ve worked really hard on that race pace and today it showed. I was extremely comfortable on the softs, pushing them.

“The car was behaving really well – apart from all the electronic downsides, I think everything was positive. In a world where we can fix our starts, I think we can have a brilliant race.”

title: Oliver Bearman questions 'crazy' stewards decision after launching F1 attack
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman has branded the stewards' decision to hand him a 10-second penalty in the United States Grand Prix as "crazy" and "very excessive."

After the early virtual safety car restart, Bearman got a run on Alpine's Pierre Gasly into the Turn 12 braking zone, and was able to position himself for a move up the inside of the following right-hander of Turn 13.

Mounting the kerb, he barged past the French driver, but the stewards immediately placed him under investigation for causing a collision.

Ultimately, Bearman was handed a 10-second penalty for the incident, which involved his front-left tyre clipping the right-hand side of Gasly's car as he made the move stick.

In the end, Bearman was forced to retire with "catastrophic" damage to his Haas machine from the incident, whilst Gasly went on to score one point for a P10 finish.

However, reflecting, Bearman was critical of the stewards' decision to penalise him, given other examples this season, and what he believed to be mitigating factors.

"I was pretty shocked, to be honest. If anything, it was a racing incident. I felt a bit hard done by for it to be a 10-second penalty as well, especially given some of the incidents that have happened this year that have gone either unpenalized or were a five-second penalty," Bearman told media, including RacingNews365.

"10 seconds for that type of incident seems very excessive, in my opinion, given what happened. I had a great start. I had a great first lap. I also had a really good VSC restart to give myself the opportunity to attack on Pierre.

"I went up the inside into Turn 13. I felt like I had enough of my car alongside to justify it and feel like I earned a bit of space, and didn't really get that space. I was climbing up onto the kerb trying to avoid contact, but I simply couldn't.

"I couldn't disappear once I decided to go for the move. I didn't lock up. I didn't lose any control. It was just that I couldn't disappear at that stage. And 10 seconds is crazy given all of those facts.

"So to be honest, the more penalising thing was that I picked up a bit of damage. It was a very small touch, but it loosened basically the floorboard, and that slowly vibrated its way off over the next few laps, and the car was just deteriorating.

"I had maybe five laps where I was actually feeling very good, and everything was fine. And then slowly, step by step, the car was getting worse, and it was game over.

"It was getting dangerous. I mean, the car was very unpredictable, and on top of that, mileage on the engine and all of the parts are important.

"It was very clear that suddenly I went from having a bit of damage on the car to having a catastrophic amount of damage on the car, and I just said: 'I'm not in this race anymore. I'm going to let Esteban go."

title: Alex Albon responds to Fernando Alonso 'back of the grid' driver gibe
excerpt:
Alex Albon insists his fight with Fernando Alonso in the United States GP was "fun" and "fair" after the Aston Martin driver landed a jab at the Williams racer.

On the opening lap, at Turn 11, Albon tried to move up the inside of Alonso at the hairpin before the back straight, but clattered into the side of the two-time champion's machine, destroying the left-hand side bargeboard and aerodynamics.

Alonso would go on to finish in 16th ahead of Albon in 17th, and speaking to the media afterwards, the veteran said that: 'We need to get better and start a bit higher up because I think the bottom of the grid, the quality of the drivers is very low at the moment."

Responding to that, Albon described what had happened in the incident, for which the stewards elected to take no action against him.

"Have you ever watched the Goodwood and see the Mustang and the Mini? Well, it was the same thing as that race," Albon replied to media, including RacingNews365, referencing a clip on YouTube of a more powerful Ford Mustang (Albon) being overtaken by a better chassis in corners [Alonso].

"Well, it was the same thing. It was fun, and it is always fun to race Fernando; he's strong, but he is always fair.

"Maybe he thought I was a bit over the edge, and I don't know; I am sure I'll find out soon enough, but I had a good amount of fun.

"It felt like there was a car on the right side of Fernando, and he gave Fernando enough space as if he thought there was only one car on his inside.

"But then I was on the inside of Fernando, and so it pinched, and I tried to get out of the way on the kerb, but I couldn't.

"So I got damage and was driving around with a broken front wing."

[Article continues below].

Albon's blue flag nightmare

Turning to the rest of his race, Albon explained his hopes of initially being able to finish well clear of the Aston Martins, but he was not able to do so.

"We pitted very early on the final set, and we had a long run on the hards," he said.

"It would have been okay, but when we came out, we were just getting blue flags, so we lost maybe 10 or 12 seconds of race time on the blue flags, and then suddenly I thought Fernando, Lance [Stroll] and team-mate Carlos [Sainz] would not be in my race.

"I knew they were in my race with a few laps to go, so I tried to hold off the Astons because I knew Carlos was on a fresher set, and tried to help him have a chance on the Astons.

"But then in the end, they got through."

title: Lando Norris was 'praying' for intervention for McLaren F1 gamble to succeed
excerpt:
Lando Norris has described how he was "praying" for a late safety car intervention to allow McLaren's strategy gamble to succeed in the United States.

Starting eighth, McLaren elected to run Norris on a one-stop strategy, with the favoured plan for cars around him being a two-stop as he cycled to second place in the closing stages.

On his worn tyres, Norris was being reeled in at great chunks by the two-stopping Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc, who ultimately got past in a double-move at Turn 1, consigning Norris to finishing off the podium.

It then got worse for the Briton, as another two-stopper, Lewis Hamilton, came past, dropping him to fifth as Norris longed for a virtual or full safety car to allow a free stop and change of tyres - something that did not come until it was too late and Valtteri Bottas's Cadillac broke down with five laps to go.

"We tried, and we were not there on pace or anything, so we had to give it a shot," Norris told media, including RacingNews365, of his one-stop attempt.

"If there was any VSC or a safety car, we were right in contention for a good podium, even P2 for a lot of it, so we were hoping, I was praying, but it never came.

"But I feel like it was a good race, the pace was strong, and I feel like I got everything out of it, so I have to be happy, even though a P5 doesn't sound amazing.

"There's not much more we can do.

"The team was debating whether to box onto different tyres or not, and I was hoping to have a better chance with the hard tyre, but it just degraded, so it was more: did we want to box and be safe and box onto another set of tyres, or did we want to stay out?

"We chose to stay out; there was no disagreement, and the team did a very good job on the strategy."

title: 2026 F1 United States Grand Prix - Austin Driver Ratings
excerpt:
Check out RacingNews365's Driver Ratings from the 2026 F1 United States Grand Prix in Austin!

Kimi Antonelli moved to the cusp of the F1 world title with a stunning performance in the United States Grand Prix.

He now just requires a ninth-place finish to be assured of the crown in Mexico City next time out - but was his performance good enough to earn a perfect 10 in our driver ratings?

And just how poor was team-mate George Russell's performance?

Read on below to find out!

© XPB Images

The top five

Kimi Antonelli - 10

Faultless. Nailed his qualifying lap out of nowhere to earn a stunning pole position, and take any danger out of the race if he'd been in the mid-pack for the start and Turn 1. Made a one-stop strategy work and won by 13s in a commanding performance. Drive of a champion.

Liam Lawson - 9.5

Maximised his result in both qualifying and the race, and played the team game by not running in Q3 to ensure Lindblad officially took P9, which would then become P14 on the grid with the penalty, instead of P15. On a weekend the top four teams all finished, ninth was the maximum possible, and he did a fantastic job to finish just 25s behind a works Mercedes - which was the fastest car in race trim - in Antonelli's hands anyway.

Charles Leclerc - 9

Dominant on Friday and made a stunning overtake on the opening lap and put manners on Verstappen into the Esses. Strong charge to come back on his two-stop and steal second place away from the Red Bull. The only blip was qualifying and the sudden track temperature changes, which rocked Ferrari - but he still got ahead of Hamilton on the grid - and made amends by passing both Red Bulls in the first 30 seconds.

Max Verstappen - 9

Was unhappy with Red Bull's strategy, but so nearly rescued second place, only to settle for third. Another strong performance and keeps the momentum building. Made up for his poor first half of the opening lap quickly by the end of it.

Pierre Gasly - 8

Like Lawson, the best Gasly could have hoped for was P10, given the big four teams all finished and Lawson's Racing Bulls was quicker than the Alpine, and kept Lawson honest.

© XPB Images

The bottom five

Carlos Sainz - 5

A difficult weekend for Williams - and Sainz gets the assigned par score. Beat his team-mate by a healthy margin in qualifying, but finished behind in the race.

Valtteri Bottas - 5

Nothing overly wrong with his performance, but just as rumours are beginning to swirl about his future, he needs to deliver more than he is showing. 0.080s slower than Perez in qualifying was good, and he was running behind in the race. Has to show more.

Franco Colapinto - 5

The par score for the Alpine driver whose race ended after 35 laps with an engine issue.

Oscar Piastri - 4.5

Eight-tenths slower than Norris in Q1, three-tenths in Q2, and was originally behind in Q3 before Norris got a time deleted for track limits, which put Piastri ahead on the grid. Got told to move out of the way of Norris as he was struggling so much, and then proceeded to finish 22s behind his team-mate on the same strategy - over a pit-stop. Does earn some credit back for keeping Russell behind for so long.

George Russell - 3

Dreadful performance, but the worrying thing is that he does not have any immediate answers about what went so badly wrong and why he is struggling. Was on the pace in Q2, but Antonelli put nearly four-and-a-half tenths on him in Q3. In the race, Antonelli finished 54.3s clear as the title race was all but ended. The penalty was extremely harsh and not deserved, and dropped him behind Piastri - but was unable to pass a McLaren which appeared not to be able to get out of its own way.

title: Toto Wolff declares Kimi Antonelli 'F1 champion' as huge statement made
excerpt:
Toto Wolff believes Kimi Antonelli's commanding performance in the United States Grand Prix was his best yet, as he declared the Italian the new world champion.

Antonelli was faultless in Austin, as he dominated the race on a one-stop strategy to ease to his ninth grand prix win of the season, nearly a minute clear of team-mate George Russell, who laboured to eighth.

The result, coupled with Lewis Hamilton taking fourth, means Antonelli must wait until Mexico to be crowned as the youngest-ever F1 champion, as he holds a 123-point lead over Russell and a 124-point buffer over Hamilton with just 125 left on the board.

It means that if Russell or Hamilton do not win in Mexico, Antonelli wins the title by default, and if either of the Britons win, Antonelli would simply require a ninth place or a 10th place, respectively, to shatter Sebastian Vettel's record from 2010 by over three years.

Reflecting on the dominant performance by the 20-year-old, Wolff felt that Antonelli had delivered a huge statement victory, and that a "tequila party" for his coronation in Mexico City was in the works.

"The main headline is that, for me, it was the best race [Antonelli] has delivered so far, in getting off the start with the inferior tyre and then controlling it at all times," Wolff told media, including RacingNews365.

"The race of a champion who isn't the champion yet, but he was exceptional, and he outperformed the car.

"Maybe it is a bit harsh to say, but I think his driving style just glues with the car, and we saw that in qualifying, where on his last lap, he could have been another tenth, or a half-a-tenth up.

"It is extremely satisfying to see what he's been able to deliver, and how he is working with the team, with Bono and yielding the results, but it wasn't an easy road.

"I'm happy to say that it is 99.9% done, but he still needs to finish the race in Mexico, so it is either going to be a tequila party, or if it is not a tequila party, then it is going to be in Sao Paulo the weekend afterwards."

[Article continues below].

Wolff explains Antonelli long road

Wolff then offered some insight into the "long road" that has seen Mercedes prepare Antonelli from karting to the cusp of the crown, including the millions spent on his career thus far.

"I wasn't the one responsible for [finding Antonelli]; it was teamwork. It was our junior team run by Gwen [Lagrue] that discovered him when he was 11," Wolff began.

"Credit to that group that have developed him over many years.

"I read an interview with Pierre Ferrari last week, where he said: "What a talent, he reminds me of Niki Lauda.'

"People don't get that this is the work of nine years, the development and hardship of nine years, the integration into the team.

"Working with the engineers and the 10 or more million spent in the development of his career, of his ability, of his character, together with his parents, and it is not that it has just landed like this.

"Many people said last year, after nine races without points, that he shouldn't be at Mercedes, and people in other teams said that he shouldn't be in Formula 1, like with the tears in parc ferme at Spa."

title: Former F1 supplier targeting stunning grand prix comeback
excerpt:
All signs point to Bridgestone entering the fray once again to attempt a return to Formula 1 as tyre supplier, RacingNews365 has learned, with other manufacturers are also eyeing Pirelli’s position.

Bridgestone is actively pushing to return to Formula 1 as a tyre supplier, RacingNews365 understands.

The Japanese manufacturer has kept a low profile, but it was present at several grands prix over the last couple of months, with its involvement becoming far more visible at the last two rounds in Singapore and the United States.

A delegation of high-level Bridgestone experts attended both races, holding background discussions about the company's planned involvement and a possible return to the sport. Bridgestone last supplied F1 at the end of 2010, before Pirelli took over as the championship's exclusive tyre supplier in 2011.

Pirelli's current deal was extended in 2023 to cover the 2025 to 2027 seasons, and the FIA activated a one-year extension option in July 2026. That means the Milan-based manufacturer is locked in as F1's tyre supplier until at least the end of the 2028 campaign.

The contract is awarded through a tender process. The FIA opens the tender, selects a winner, and then makes a proposal to Formula 1 to begin commercial and business negotiations before finalising the deal.

[Article continues below]

© xpb.cc

A Japanese key F1 figure

Sources with insight into the matter, when asked by RacingNews365, give Bridgestone a strong chance of being the next selected manufacturer.

It is understood that the Japanese company is preparing to return to F1 with a technological, business and commercial package that is stronger compared to its previous bid, which was already widely considered to be robust.

During its first spell in F1, Bridgestone competed between 1997 and 2006 in a tyre war with Michelin, before becoming the exclusive supplier in 2007 until its withdrawal four seasons later after the 2010 campaign.

Bridgestone restructured its motorsport division in 2025 and signed a key figure, Hiroshi Imai, to lead the organisation, signalling its F1 intentions.

Imai, re-signed by Bridgestone after a previous spell between 1990 and 2008 before he left to join McLaren, was a member of the company's high-level delegation at the races in Singapore and Austin.

Imai worked at McLaren from 2009 to 2025, serving as chief race engineer, suspension and brakes performance director, and in his final years, director of race engineering. He was highly respected at the Woking team, where his departure was viewed as a significant loss.

Several of RacingNews365's paddock sources have stated that the company's F1 ambitions were behind "luring" back Imai.

However, they also noted that the technological standards are strong enough for F1, as the company is active in numerous high-level racing series.

Bridgestone took over as the exclusive tyre supplier for Formula E for the 2026–27 season, and is present in IndyCar through its Firestone brand. It also competes in Super GT and other series.

[Article continues below]

© xpb.cc

Other suppliers also interested

Although our sources suggest that Bridgestone's bid will be even stronger than last time, a serious battle could unfold for the role of tyre supplier.

The pinnacle of motor racing gives the selected company an unrivalled opportunity to develop and demonstrate its technology level, as well as worldwide premium visibility and an incomparable marketing platform.

It is highly likely that more companies will be interested in the role.

Despite its decade-and-a-half presence, it cannot be ruled out that Pirelli will try to continue. According to our information, other manufacturers are also preparing for the tender.

Hankook's interest has been well known for some time, but there are also rumours that even Michelin might take a shot at the challenge.

title: George Russell seeking Mercedes investigation as title end-game nears
excerpt:
George Russell is intending to "dig deep" into the data with his Mercedes engineers to understand why he was so slow in the United States, as the title race all but ended.

With team-mate Kimi Antonelli scoring a crushing victory, Russell was required to finish at least eighth to extend the fight to Mexico City - which is where he finished following a poor weekend, having failed to overtake McLaren's Oscar Piastri for most of the race.

Russell dropped behind the Australian after a "ridiculous" five-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage on the opening lap, and Antonelli victory and Russell's eighth place mean the Italian now has a 123-point advantage over the Briton.

If Russell does not win in Mexico, Antonelli will be champion by default, with the 20-year-old just requiring a ninth-place finish to be assured of the crown.

Reflecting on the race that all but extinguished his faint hopes of the title, Russell was initially asked about his penalty and whether getting stuck behind Piastri had "compromised" his race.

"The pace wasn't good in the first stint, and when I came out of the pits on the hards, I probably did six laps on the same pace as Kimi, but then I caught up to Oscar, and I just couldn't overtake, so six good laps, 50 bad laps," Russell began to media, including RacingNews365.

"I want to understand why the pace was so bad in the first stint; the penalty was a bit ridiculous, but that was the least of my worries after such a bad weekend."

After a recent breakthrough with his dominant win in Azerbaijan, Russell has once again struggled in recent weeks to match Antonelli's performances, and indicated that he needed time to process the apparent backward steps.

"I don't have the answers right now, and I need to give it 24 hours to think clearly," he added, before going on to express his intention of 'digging deep' with his engineers to try and find a solution on how to extract lap-time from the upgraded W17 machine.

"The window [with the car] is narrow, and we saw in Malaysia, [Antonelli] was quickest in FP3 and then we qualified fourth and eighth, and then this weekend, we were both up there in Q2, and then I was nowhere in Q3 and nowhere in the race," he said.

"He was obviously exceptionally competitive, and there are signs the window is very small.

"I hope that's an explanation for my lack of pace, but I need to dig deep with my team because it is difficult to understand when you are so far off."

[Article continues below]

Russell's end-game approaches

With the endgame nearing in the championship, the fight for second has closed right up, with Russell in second now just nine points ahead of Charles Leclerc in fifth, with Hamilton and Max Verstappen between.

Looking ahead to the rest of the season, Russell declared his sole aim was to help Mercedes win a ninth constructors' crown.

"For me, as long as we win the constructors', that's the main thing," Russell added.

"I'd like to finish as best of the rest, but P2, P3, P5 is not the champion, so it doesn't mean anything."

title: Max Verstappen makes 'sign language' proposal after latest radio 'disaster'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen claims he has lost count of how many times Red Bull's radio system has failed him this season after yet another communication breakdown during the United States Grand Prix.

Verstappen finished third at Circuit of the Americas, behind race winner Kimi Antonelli and Charles Leclerc, but was left fuming at a recurring problem that has dogged his car on multiple occasions in 2026.

Asked how frustrating it was to suffer another radio dropout, and that it was not the first time this year, Verstappen did not hold back.

"It's not the second time," said Verstappen, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "It's already, I don't know how many times this year.

"Maybe we should just start communicating in sign language. It's probably cheaper as well.

"It's a disaster. Yeah, it's a disaster. It's really frustrating, to be honest."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen - 'Hurts your performance'

Verstappen's frustration was not limited to the communication issues. The four-time F1 champion also pointed to strategic errors and a slow pit stop that cost him time in his battle for the podium places.

Notably, Red Bull deployed a two-stop strategy for the race, running soft-soft-medium, which Verstappen has claimed was "not agreed" beforehand.

Asked whether more was possible from the car given the problems, Verstappen said Red Bull had failed to extract the maximum from the weekend.

"Today we didn't maximise much," said Verstappen.

"The issues, of course, don't help, but I think also the strategy that we did with the tyre choices that we made, they were just not good.

"So that's a few things to analyse: why these tyres didn't work as we expected, or why the other tyres performed better than expected. So something to learn from.

"And then, the slow pit stop doesn't help as well. It's just seconds that you throw away, right? When you're fighting a close battle for second, that hurts your performance.

"Normally we're very good at these things, but today we weren't."

title: Fernando Alonso slates 'back of the grid' drivers after Alex Albon collision
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has hit out at the driving standards amongst the midfield and backmarker runners after an opening-lap collision with Alex Albon wrecked his United States Grand Prix.

The two-time F1 champion made contact with the Williams driver at Turn 11 on lap one at the Circuit of the Americas, destroying the bargeboard on the left-hand side of his Aston Martin, leading to a loss of downforce and a 16th-place finish at the chequered flag.

Stewards opted against handing Albon a penalty for the clash, treating it as a standard first-lap racing incident.

Speaking after the race, however, Alonso did not hold back when assessing the manoeuvre that triggered the damage.

Asked for his view on the incident, Alonso said: "That Albon forgot that corner 11 was there, and he had to turn left."

Pulling no punches, he added: "We need to get better and start a bit higher up because I think the bottom of the grid, the quality of the drivers is very low at the moment."

[Article continues below]

Alonso - 'Ruined on the first lap'

The 45-year-old explained just how much the contact cost him over the remaining 55 laps in Austin.

"It compromised [the race] a lot," he said. "I think we had more than half a second of damage on the car every lap, and even with that, I think we were quite competitive."

Despite the setback, Alonso rated his underlying pace as amongst the strongest of his campaign.

"By far the best race of the season from my point of view," he added. "Probably we could have been in the points on merit, maybe P10, P9, something like that.

"Definitely a very good weekend ruined on the first lap, but nothing we can do now."

title: Kimi Antonelli reveals 'blocking out the noise' tactics to F1 title success
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has credited the people around him for helping him "block out the noise" as he closes in on a maiden F1 title following a commanding victory at the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

Antonelli's triumph has moved him to the brink of becoming the youngest champion in Formula 1 history, with the 20-year-old now in a position to clinch the title on Sunday in Mexico City.

The 20-year-old has a 123-point cushion over his nearest challenger, Mercedes team-mate George Russell, after taking his ninth win of the season, and with five races remaining.

The Italian has faced mounting scrutiny as the title fight has intensified, but says a tight circle has kept him grounded throughout.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, after the race, Antonelli explained how he has managed the pressure.

"To be fair, I'm very lucky because I have a very good group of people around me," said the young Italian.

"In the team, I have my father, who always comes, and then my performance coach. I just have a great group of people around me who help me to be more relaxed and not worry about these kinds of things.

"They help me to block out the noise, and that's also what's been allowing me to enjoy the weekend and perform.

"Obviously, there's been a lot of talk. I'm not going to lie, on Thursday there was a lot of talk about the championship and stuff, and I just tried not to worry about that at all and deliver the best result I could.

"This was a very important result for me and for the team."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli - Upgrade still a work in progress

Antonelli's win came despite Mercedes still fine-tuning the upgrade package introduced back in Sepang, which brought a reworked floor and sidepods but also introduced some front-end locking under braking.

Asked whether that upgrade was now delivering the pace he and the team had expected all along, Antonelli gave a mixed verdict.

"In some places, I would say, still not as much as we expected, but in other places it is delivering very well," he said.

"I think in the high- and medium-speed the car is very strong. The balance is good. But we're still struggling a little bit at low speed with front locking.

"Overall, I feel like the package is finally starting to deliver, and we're starting to see the results and the improvements from the package."

title: Irritated Max Verstappen criticises Red Bull: 'That wasn't agreed'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has launched a scathing attack on Red Bull's strategy calls after salvaging third place at the United States Grand Prix, insisting "this was not what we agreed" when it came to his tyre choices.

Verstappen had hoped to fight for victory from second on the grid at the Circuit of the Americas, but Kimi Antonelli proved untouchable up front.

The Dutchman ran a two-stop strategy and had to fend off a late charge from the Ferraris, eventually losing second to Charles Leclerc before narrowly holding off Lewis Hamilton to secure the final podium spot, having been aided by the late Valtteri Bottas-induced virtual safety car.

Despite the result, the four-time F1 drivers' champion was far from satisfied, telling Viaplay that very little had gone to plan.

"I've had more enjoyable races," Verstappen said. "Not that much really went well. The start wasn't good, and neither was the way we handled the tyre choice. Soft, soft, medium — that wasn't agreed beforehand. I don't really understand why that happened."

"I also had too many problems with the engine, but that was already the case in qualifying. Just really inconsistent.

"One corner there's not enough engine braking, so it just carries on through, and then the next one it's suddenly really aggressive.

"Another moment it wasn't shifting properly. I can't make sense of it. I'm not going to complain every lap, but it just wasn't good. The whole weekend wasn't good, and in the race it was even worse."

Hard tyre left unused

Verstappen also pointed to the pace of the hard compound, which he never got the chance to use.

"They didn't put that on my car," the 29-year-old said. "That's not what we'd agreed.

"Everyone immediately knows you're doing a two-stopper [once you switch back to softs]. We'd agreed on the medium, but I need to have a word about it. No idea why it happened that way."

The Red Bull driver said the car's inconsistency ran through the entire weekend.

"The balance of the car wasn't optimal, but there were also too many issues," he added. "You just can't drive with any consistency when something's different every single time. Every lap, every corner, it's just not consistent."

Asked about settling for third rather than fighting Leclerc for second, Verstappen shrugged off the distinction, concluding: "It doesn't make that much difference whether you're third or fourth.

"When they told me how close Lewis Hamilton was behind me and how much he was catching per lap, there was no point fighting Charles, because then I'd have lost that position too."

title: Lewis Hamilton offers 'crazy' Ferrari explanation after USGP podium miss
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton failed in a late charge for a podium in the United States GP.

Lewis Hamilton has offered a "crazy" explanation for missing out on a podium at the United States Grand Prix, revealing that Ferrari spent much of the weekend chasing the wrong set-up before correcting course too late to catch Max Verstappen for third place.

The seven-time world champion finished fourth at the Circuit of the Americas, 18.515 seconds behind race winner Kimi Antonelli, with Charles Leclerc taking second and Verstappen completing the podium in third.

Hamilton said his struggles traced back to Friday, when Ferrari ran the wrong set-up in FP1 before heading further off course in FP2.

"I think I was lacking pace in the first two stints," Hamilton told select media, including RacingNews365. "Basically, I just couldn't turn the car, and I think ultimately it all kind of started on Friday.

"Wrong set-up, really, for FP1, and then went the wrong direction in FP2. Reverted back and got to a better place for FP3. But there's a subtle difference between Charles and me and our car, basically just in the race, and it's just to do mostly with flap, how much wing you put in, and I think we've just been under-hitting it, continuously under-hitting it for some reason.

"When you do the lap to the grid, it feels like the car is good, and then as soon as the race starts, massive washout and understeer, and I couldn't do anything about it, so they just pulled away. I lost those eight seconds, and that's really why I didn't get that position [on Verstappen] in the end."

Lewis Hamilton reveals constant Ferrari pit stop adjustments

By FP3, Hamilton had begun converging towards the same direction as Leclerc's car, but the pair still started the race on noticeably different wing levels.

Hamilton went into Sunday's race with less front wing than his teammate, leaving him short of the load Leclerc had already built up through a long run completed in FP2.

That gap forced Ferrari into reactive adjustments throughout the afternoon, with Hamilton needing repeated flap changes at his pit stops just to bring the balance closer to where Leclerc's car had started.

Asked how he became so quick by the end of the race, Hamilton explained the scale of the correction required.

"Because through the pit stops, I added four clicks," began explaining Hamilton. "The next pit stop added another four clicks, and even then, I'm still another four clicks too short. And it's crazy, like, to be 12 clicks down. We really need to look at how we get to that point.

"But I think it would have been a bit different if we had started with it. I think in FP2, where we did the long run, that's where Charles got the experience on that set-up, and I didn't get the long run on it. So, a bit of a back step on it. Lots of positives to take.

"The team did a really great job with pit stops and the strategy, and we obviously had decent pace today, particularly the last stint. If I had that in the first two, we would have for sure been on the podium, I think."
